content: Gastritis refers to the inflammation of the stomach lining, medically known as the gastric mucosa. The term gastritis originates from the Greek words gastromeaning stomach and -itis meaning inflammation. Depending on the underlying cause, gastritis can manifest as either an acute or chronic condition. In some cases, it may progress to more severe conditions, such as gastric atrophy. The term gastritis was first introduced in 1728 by German physician Georg Ernst Stahl to describe inflammation of the stomach lining. In 1982, Robin Warren and Barry Marshall discovered Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori), a bacterium that significantly advanced the understanding, classification, and diagnosis of various types of gastritis. By 2005, the OLGA (Operative Link on Gastritis Assessment) staging system was introduced to standardize the reporting of gastric histology and assess the progression of gastritis. Acute gastritis, also known as reactive gastritis, is often triggered by factors such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), stress, bile reflux, radiation, excessive alcohol consumption, cocaine use, or ischemic damage. The acute phase is typically subclinical and lasts for a short duration, approximately 7 to 10 days. Chronic gastritis, on the other hand, is frequently associated with persistent H. pylori infection, which leads to the accumulation of chronic inflammatory cells and the development of active chronic gastritis. Gastritis must be distinguished from other gastrointestinal conditions, such as peptic ulcer disease, gastric cancer, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), Crohn's disease, gastrinoma, gastric adenocarcinoma, and primary gastric lymphoma. Globally, the prevalence of H. pylori infection varies widely, with higher rates observed in developing countries. In the United States, H. pylori-associated gastritis is more common among African Americans, Hispanics, and the elderly compared to Whites. Risk factors for gastritis include alcohol consumption, prolonged NSAID use, cocaine use, autoimmune gastritis, Crohn's disease, HIV/AIDS, and bacterial infections such as H. pylori. Less common risk factors include food poisoning, vitamin B12 deficiency due to autoimmune gastritis, stress from major surgery or trauma, bile reflux, low-fiber diets, pernicious anemia, and infections caused by viruses, parasites, or fungi. Routine screening for gastritis is not currently recommended due to insufficient evidence. However, individuals with persistent gastritis are at an increased risk of developing complications such as peptic ulcers, gastrointestinal bleeding, gastric polyps, anemia, vitamin B12 deficiency, and, in severe cases, gastric cancer. The prognosis of gastritis depends on its type and underlying cause. Acute gastritis often resolves with the cessation of risk factors such as NSAIDs, alcohol, and smoking. Chronic gastritis associated with H. pylori infection generally has a good prognosis when treated appropriately. However, untreated H. pylori-associated gastritis can progress to peptic ulcer disease, gastric adenocarcinoma, or MALT lymphoma. Symptoms of gastritis may range from silent to overt, including abdominal discomfort, nausea, vomiting, gastrointestinal bleeding, bloating, belching, heartburn, loss of appetite, and fatigue. Physical examination findings may include pallor, fatigue, epigastric tenderness, and, in cases of gastrointestinal bleeding, tachycardia or melena. Diagnostic evaluation of gastritis often involves endoscopic methods, including biopsy for histology, rapid urease testing, culture, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Non-invasive tests, such as antibody tests, urea breath tests, and fecal antigen tests, are also used to detect H. pylori. Imaging studies, such as CT scans and X-rays (e.g., barium swallow), may aid in diagnosis by identifying gastric wall edema or ulcers. Treatment of gastritis depends on its etiology. Medications that contribute to gastritis, such as NSAIDs, should be discontinued. Lifestyle modifications, including smoking cessation and abstinence from alcohol, are recommended. Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) are commonly prescribed to reduce gastric acid production. For H. pylori infection, antimicrobial therapy is essential. Triple therapy (PPI, clarithromycin, and amoxicillin or metronidazole) and quadruple therapy (PPI, bismuth subsalicylate, metronidazole, and tetracycline) are effective regimens, with the latter achieving success rates exceeding 90%. Primary prevention strategies for gastritis include avoiding long-term NSAID use, alcohol, smoking, and acidic or spicy foods. Maintaining a healthy diet, regular exercise, and stress management are also beneficial. Secondary prevention involves eradicating H. pylori infection to prevent recurrence of peptic ulcers and reduce the risk of gastric cancer. Surgical intervention is not typically recommended for the management of gastritis.
